title: Progress and Prospect of AI in ARPES Workflow
authors: Sandy Adhitia Ekahana, Aalok Tiwari, Pratik Saud, Aaron Bostwick, Chris Jozwiak, Eli Rotenberg, Jyoti Katoch
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly useful tool across the experimental sciences, including angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which routinely produces large, multidimensional datasets of electronic structure. Recent advances in AI and machine learning (ML) have opened new opportunities across the entire ARPES workflow, from automated sample preparation and real-time data acquisition to post-experiment data analysis and comparison with theoretical calculations. Despite this progress, a comprehensive review of ML applications, their capabilities, and reliability across the different stages of ARPES workflow is still lacking. In this review, we first introduce ML methods that are most relevant to experimentalists working in condensed matter physics and materials science. We then follow the ARPES workflow, reviewing existing ML applications at each step and discussing their advantages, limitations and potential for future development. We also examine the current ARPES data landscape, where several open databases are available but remain relatively small and fragmented compared with large, shared datasets such as ImageNet. Given these limitations, we suggest that the community focus on sharing pretrained models that can be further trained, adapted to specific tasks, and redistributed, while working toward a larger and standardized open ARPES dataset repository. Finally, we discuss our perspectives on the future of AI within the ARPES workflow using a six-level framework of laboratory automation, highlighting the opportunities and challenges in moving toward a fully autonomous, self-driving ARPES laboratory.
summary: This review surveys the rapidly expanding role of AI and ML in the Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) workflow. It details how ML is applied across all stages, from sample preparation to advanced data inversion, highlighting the move toward autonomous, closed-loop experimental systems. The paper stresses the urgent need for standardized, large-scale open datasets to accelerate this progress.
main_problem: The field requires a comprehensive review and advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) applications across the entire Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) workflow due to the large, multidimensional datasets produced.
main_result: The paper reviews ML applications across the entire ARPES workflow, suggesting a community focus on sharing pretrained models and developing a standardized, large open ARPES dataset repository.
method: The review systematically examines ML techniques (Deep Learning, PINNs, etc.) applied to various stages of the ARPES process, from sample preparation to data analysis and autonomous control.
model_or_system: The primary system is ARPES, which measures the occupied electronic band structure of crystalline materials, generating high-dimensional datasets. The workflow spans sample growth, measurement, and analysis, increasingly aiming for closed-loop, autonomous operation.
key_observables: Electronic band dispersion ($\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}$), electron self-energy ($\Sigma(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$), and photoemission intensity $I(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$.
important_parameters:
Photon energy ($h
u$), binding energy ($E_B$), and momentum ($\mathbf{k}$).
main_assumptions: Current open ARPES databases are small and fragmented compared to large datasets like ImageNet, limiting the scope of ML training.
figures_summary: The figures schematically illustrate the entire ARPES workflow, showing the progression from sample growth through measurement to analysis, emphasizing the closed-loop nature enabled by AI.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a comprehensive review, first introducing relevant ML methods, then following the physical ARPES workflow stages (sample prep, measurement, analysis) to review existing applications, and concluding with future perspectives on laboratory automation.
why_interesting: The integration of ML into interpreting complex, high-dimensional spectroscopic data like ARPES spectra is crucial for extracting fundamental electronic structure information, which is relevant to understanding many-body physics and correlated systems.
